analysis.one_liner: Bans betting on wars, assassinations, terrorism, and government decisions.
analysis.headline: Sen. Chris Murphy's bill to ban wagers on wars, assassinations, and government actions has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since its referral in March 2026, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The BETS OFF Act makes it illegal for anyone to place, accept, or facilitate bets on an act of terrorism, an assassination, a war, or a government action whose outcome one person fully controls or already knows in advance. It tells exchanges regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission that they may not list such event contracts, lets the Attorney General sue to stop violations, and tucks the ban into existing federal gambling and racketeering laws. It explicitly does not touch insurance, flood, crop, or terrorism insurance. The bill was introduced March 17, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has remained with no further action [S1] [S2] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who do not want markets where insiders profit from national security events. The ban targets wagers on events whose outcome is 'known by any person in advance' or 'under the complete control of any person' — the situations where a government official, contractor, or other insider could cash in on information the public does not have, or where a bettor profits directly from a tragedy. It also protects the integrity of government decisions by removing a financial market that rewards particular outcomes [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to place, accept, or facilitate any wager on a 'specified event' — an act of terrorism, an assassination, a war, or a government action whose outcome is completely controlled by, or already known to, any person [S2].

Amends the Commodity Exchange Act so that no CFTC-regulated exchange or clearinghouse may list or clear contracts on these specified events, closing the main venue where such markets now operate [S2].

Adds the prohibition to existing federal gambling statutes — the Travel Act, the Illegal Gambling Business Act, and the Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act — and allows the Attorney General to seek a court injunction against violators [S2].
Explicitly exempts legitimate insurance, including terrorism insurance, flood insurance, and crop insurance, so it bans profiteering wagers without disrupting genuine risk coverage [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Prediction-market platforms and exchanges lose the revenue from markets on wars, elections of government action, assassinations, and similar events — the category that has driven much of their recent growth. Bettors lose the option to wager on these events [S2].

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is limited: the Attorney General may only seek an injunction; the bill creates no direct criminal penalty or fines for violating the prohibition itself, though the conduct can be folded into existing gambling and racketeering statutes [S2].

The definition is broad — it covers any government action 'the primary underlying characteristic of which is not financial, commercial, or economic' whose outcome one person fully controls — which critics could argue reaches well beyond the headline events and chills lawful event markets [S2].

A good-faith objection to any such ban is that prediction markets are said to aggregate information and forecast events; banning wagers on wars and government actions removes that channel, though on events where insiders hold decisive information such markets mainly reward those insiders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — keeping markets from letting insiders profit on terrorism, assassination, war, and secret government decisions — is real but narrow; the cost falls mainly on a young industry's ability to list those specific contracts. The bill is carefully drafted to leave ordinary insurance alone. The main weakness is light enforcement: an injunction-only remedy gives the government limited tools if platforms move offshore.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on March 17, 2026, and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since — it is sitting in committee while Congress remains in session [S1] [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT), joined by Sen. John Hickenlooper, introduced the BETS OFF Act on March 17, 2026 [S1] [S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary — its only action to date [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no committee action has been scheduled [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, prediction-market platforms and exchanges: the wagering they offer on wars, assassinations, and government actions continues unrestricted while the bill sits without a hearing. Nobody gains or loses materially yet beyond the status quo. If the bill never moves, the platforms are the clear winners and the public never gets the protections the bill would provide.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the BETS OFF Act to ban wagers on terrorism, assassination, war, and government actions.

for.name: Sen. John Hickenlooper
for.what_they_did: Joined Murphy in introducing the bill at introduction.

for.name: Second Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as one of the bill's two cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors are Democrats, so the bill has so far drawn only one-party support; no one has publicly opposed it and no vote has occurred, so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: These platforms make money listing contracts on events like wars, government strikes, and other sensitive events; the bill bars CFTC-registered exchanges from listing or clearing contracts on those specified events. Their revenue on these markets comes from letting people bet on outcomes of national security and government decisions, an interest that runs against the public interest in keeping such events free of financial profiteering — particularly by insiders who know outcomes in advance [S2].

The bill explicitly excludes lawful insurance — including the federal terrorism, flood, and crop insurance programs and reinsurance — so legitimate insurance business is untouched. The insurance industry has no stake against the ban [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in the Senate Judiciary Committee since its referral with only two cosponsors, and no hearing or markup has been scheduled. Most private member bills at this stage die in committee without a vote, and this one would need its chairman to act and a broader coalition to build; its prospects this Congress are poor unless event-contract controversies force the issue onto the committee agenda.
